47938: Originals and Translations: The Full Picture
47939: Is a literal translation always right? What do we miss when the Bible moves from Hebrew and Greek into English or Tamil, and how did our Bibles come to be?
47940: Every translation is also an interpretation. Word-for-word versions keep the form, meaning-for-meaning versions carry the sense, and both lose something. Idioms read literally can mislead, and some words carry more than any single English or Tamil word can hold, so wise readers use more than one translation and learn the key words.
47941: God's word was made to travel
47942:
Unless you read Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek, every Bible you have read is a translation. That is not a modern weakness; it is built into the Bible's own story. When Ezra read the Law, the Levites 'gave the sense, so that the people understood the reading' (Neh 8:8), possibly by explaining it in Aramaic. Jesus mostly spoke Aramaic, yet the Gospels record his words in Greek, keeping only a few Aramaic phrases such as *Talitha koum* (Mark 5:41). The New Testament writers often quote the Old Testament from the Greek Septuagint translation.

At Pentecost the crowd heard the apostles 'each in his own native language' (Acts 2:6-11). God did not make everyone learn one holy language first. The Christian message has spread by being translated, which the historian Lamin Sanneh saw as one of its defining features. A Tamil-speaking believer reading the Tamil Bible is not reading a second-class Bible.

The flip side is that translation always involves choices. No two languages match word for word, so translators must decide again and again whether to keep the form of the original or to carry its meaning in natural speech.
47943: Word for word, meaning for meaning, or paraphrase
47944:
Translations sit along a spectrum. At one end is *formal equivalence*, often called word-for-word. It keeps the original's words, word order and images as closely as natural English allows. Examples are the KJV, NASB, NKJV and ESV. The Tamil Union Version (the 'O.V.') also leans this way.

At the other end is *functional equivalence* (also called dynamic equivalence), thought-for-thought translation. The term comes from the linguist Eugene Nida. It aims to have the same effect on today's readers that the original had on its first readers, using natural modern speech. Examples are the Good News Bible, the NLT and the CEV. In the middle are versions that try to balance the two, such as the NIV, CSB and NET.

Beyond the spectrum is *paraphrase*: a free retelling in contemporary language by one person, such as Kenneth Taylor's *Living Bible* or Eugene Peterson's *The Message*. Paraphrases can make familiar words come alive, but they carry more of the writer's own interpretation and are not meant as study Bibles.

Even the most literal translation interprets. Translators must decide what each word means in its context, how to handle Hebrew and Greek grammar, and when an English word has changed its meaning over time.
47945: Idioms that mislead when translated literally
47946:
An *idiom* is a phrase whose meaning is not the sum of its words, like 'kick the bucket' in English. Hebrew and Greek have many. Read literally, without their cultural context, they can mean something quite different to us.

Paul tells his readers to feed their enemies, 'for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head' (Rom 12:20, KJV, quoting Prov 25:21-22). Read literally it sounds like revenge. Most scholars think it means your kindness will cause the enemy burning shame or remorse that may lead to change, which fits the next verse: 'overcome evil with good' (Rom 12:21). Some connect it to an Egyptian ritual of carrying coals as a sign of repentance; that theory is debated.

The KJV's 'bowels of mercies' (Col 3:12) translates the Greek *splanchna*, the inner organs, which ancient people saw as the seat of deep feeling, much as we speak of the heart. It means heartfelt compassion. When Jesus says 'if thine eye be single' and warns against an 'evil eye' (Matt 6:22-23), he uses a Jewish idiom: a 'good eye' is generosity and an 'evil eye' is stinginess (Deut 15:9; Prov 22:9; Matt 20:15). The verses around it are about money (Matt 6:19-24). And 'hate' your father and mother (Luke 14:26) is a Semitic way of saying 'love less by comparison', as Matt 10:37 makes clear. A pure word-for-word translation keeps these images but may hide their meaning; a meaning-based one makes the sense clear but loses the picture.
47947: Words that will not fit in one word
47948:
Some words carry a whole world. The Hebrew *hesed* combines love, loyalty, mercy and covenant faithfulness: love that keeps its promises when it does not have to. English Bibles render it 'mercy', 'lovingkindness', 'steadfast love' or 'unfailing love'. The Tamil Union Version often uses கிருபை (*kirubai*, grace or mercy), as in the refrain of Psalm 136.

*Shalom* is more than the absence of war. It means wholeness, health, prosperity and right relationships, which is why Jeremiah could tell exiles to seek the *shalom* (welfare) of Babylon (Jer 29:7). Tamil சமாதானம் (*samādhānam*) and English 'peace' both catch only part of it. *Nephesh* is often translated 'soul', but in Genesis 2:7 the man does not receive a soul; he *becomes* a living *nephesh*, a living being. It can mean life, throat, appetite or the whole person, so 'soul' (Tamil ஆத்துமா, *āttumā*) can wrongly suggest only an invisible part of us.

In Paul, the Greek *sarx* ('flesh') can mean the body, human weakness, or life organised against God (Rom 8:4-9). A single word, whether English 'flesh' or Tamil மாம்சம் (*māmsam*), cannot show which sense is meant. *Dikaiosynē* covers both 'righteousness' and 'justice', which English splits into two words. Tamil நீதி (*nīti*) keeps the two together, as Greek does. When you meet such words, the best response is not to find the perfect translation but to study how the word is used across Scripture.
47949:
English translation began with John Wycliffe's followers, who translated from the Latin Vulgate around 1382. William Tyndale produced the first printed English New Testament translated from Greek (1526), and was executed for his work in 1536. Coverdale's Bible (1535), the Great Bible (1539), the Geneva Bible (1560, with study notes) and the Bishops' Bible (1568) followed.

At the Hampton Court Conference in 1604, King James I agreed to a new translation. About 47 scholars worked in six companies at Westminster, Oxford and Cambridge, revising the Bishops' Bible and comparing the Hebrew and Greek and earlier versions. Much of their wording comes from Tyndale. The KJV appeared in 1611, including the Apocrypha, with marginal notes giving alternative renderings. Most KJVs printed today follow Benjamin Blayney's Oxford edition of 1769, which updated spelling and corrected errors.

The KJV shaped the English language and generations of faith. Its limits are also real: its New Testament follows the Textus Receptus (Lesson 3), and some words have changed meaning. 'Let' meant hinder (2 Thess 2:7), 'prevent' meant go before (1 Thess 4:15), and 'conversation' meant way of life (Phil 1:27). The translators themselves said in their preface that a variety of translations is profitable for finding the sense of Scripture.
47951:
The Tamil Bible has one of the earliest Protestant translation histories in Asia. Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg, a German Lutheran missionary of the Danish-Halle Mission, arrived at Tranquebar (Tharangambadi) in 1706. He learned Tamil, set up a printing press, and printed the Tamil New Testament in two parts in 1714 and 1715, the first New Testament printed in an Indian language. By his death in 1719 he had translated the Old Testament as far as Ruth; Benjamin Schultze completed it, printed in 1728.

Johann Philipp Fabricius, working in Madras from the 1740s, revised these translations with a gift for good Tamil. His New Testament appeared in 1758 (revised 1766) and his Old Testament was published in 1798, after his death in 1791. Tamil Lutherans used his version for generations. In the nineteenth century C. T. E. Rhenius translated a new New Testament (1833), Peter Percival in Jaffna produced a 'Tentative Version' (1850) with the help of the Tamil scholar Arumuka Navalar, and a committee led by Henry Bower prepared another revision. After disagreements between Indian and Ceylonese churches, a jointly agreed text, the Union Version, was published in 1871. It became the standard Tamil Protestant Bible, today published by the Bible Society of India and often called the 'O.V.' (Old Version).

In 1995 Catholic and Protestant scholars together produced a common-language translation, the திருவிவிலியம் (*Thiruviviliam*). It prefers words of Tamil origin to the Sanskrit-derived words common in the O.V. For example, the O.V. usually says தேவன் (*Tēvaṉ*) for God, பரிசுத்த ஆவி (*Parisutta Āvi*) for the Holy Spirit and கர்த்தர் (*Karttar*) for the LORD, while the Thiruviviliam uses கடவுள் (*Kaṭavuḷ*), தூய ஆவியார் (*Tūya Āviyār*) and ஆண்டவர் (*Āṇṭavar*). John 1:1 reads 'ஆதியிலே வார்த்தை இருந்தது' in the O.V. and 'தொடக்கத்தில் வாக்கு இருந்தது' in the Thiruviviliam. Easy-to-read Tamil versions and revised editions of the O.V. have followed. Like English readers comparing the KJV and NIV, Tamil readers gain much by reading the O.V. alongside a modern version.
